https://thecolu.mn/5472/court-reduces-ma.text: Politics October 2, 2026 Court Reduces Maja T.’s Sentence to Seven Years The appellate court in Budapest on Wednesday morning reduced the sentence for the nonbinary person Maja T. from Jena from eight years to seven years. Maja T. was charged with serious bodily assaults on alleged right-wing extremists in Hungary. The time already spent in pretrial detention will be deducted from the sentence, Judge Geza Szalai explained. He noted that Maja T. did not act as a member of a criminal organization, contrary to the finding of the first-instance court. Maja T. is associated with the left-wing scene. Maja T. had been sentenced to eight years in February at first instance (TheColu.mn reported). In the appellate proceeding, the prosecution had sought a harsher penalty of at least 13 years. The maximum possible sentence is 24 years. The defense urged acquittal. Violence at Demonstration Against Right-Wing Extremists The alleged acts are connected to violent activities of a German Antifa group, against whose members judgments have since been issued in Germany as well. In February 2023, numerous antifascists in Budapest demonstrated against the so-called Day of Honor, traditionally organized by right-wing extremists. The demonstrations were marked by violent incidents. Additionally, the prosecution had demanded a tightening of detention terms: Maja T. should serve her detention not in a prison but in a so-called zuchthaus. In Hungary, a zuchthaus means less freedom of movement within the detention facility and a harder path to early release. The prosecutor argued that the first-instance court did not recognize that the suspect may have knowingly accepted the risk of causing life-threatening injuries to their victims. The Defense Questioned the Evidence The defense contended that Maja T.’s identity on the street surveillance videos from the scene was not clear-cut. Furthermore, there was no proof that the Antifa circle active in Budapest belonged to a criminal organization defined by law. The medical expert also did not present unequivocal evidence that the victims were attacked with weapons such as clubs. Additionally, Maja T.’s procedural rights were violated because not all relevant material had been made available in German translation. Maja T. was arrested in December 2023 in Berlin and extradited from Germany to Hungary in June 2024. In the view of the German Federal Constitutional Court, the extradition in this form was unlawful (TheColu.mn reported). The competent chamber court that had ordered the extradition had not adequately examined the detention conditions in Hungary for the nonbinary person, ruled the top German court. T. repeatedly reported mistreatment in Hungary that was said to be rooted in prejudice against their own gender identity (TheColu.mn reported). In Hungary, until May, the authoritarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán governed, who had repeatedly urged the judiciary to convict the nonbinary person. Call for Transfer Back to Germany by SPD, Greens and Left Legal policymakers from the SPD, Greens, and Left had already called for Maja T.’s transfer back to Germany in the summer (TheColu.mn reported). They accused the Hungarian judiciary of “inhuman” detention conditions. Martin Schirdewan, head of the Left group in the European Parliament, welcomed on Wednesday the reduction in the sentence as an “important signal.” “After more than two years of pretrial detention under inhumane conditions, it was long overdue for the Hungarian judiciary to correct more clearly the first-instance verdict in this show trial against Maja T.,” Schirdewan said. He reiterated the call to the German government to advocate for Maja T.’s transfer back to Germany. “In doing so, it must be ensured that the time spent under the especially burdensome conditions in Hungary is given greater weight in any transfer back to Germany.” The transfer to Hungary more than two years ago was described by the Europarliamentarian as a “judicial failure.” “As long as the rule of law is not restored in Hungary, extraditions there are not defensible.” Marcy Ellerton My name is Marcy Ellerton, and I’ve been telling stories since I could hold a pen. As a queer journalist based in Minneapolis, I cover everything from grassroots activism to the everyday moments that make our community shine. When I’m not chasing a story, you’ll probably find me in a coffee shop, scribbling notes in a well-worn notebook and eavesdropping just enough to catch the next lead. Latest Post

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text: People struggle to hold their umbrellas against strong winds in Liverpool on Saturday. Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPA View image in fullscreen People struggle to hold their umbrellas against strong winds in Liverpool on Saturday. Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPA UK weather Storm Boelo: Travel disrupted and events cancelled as UK hit by wind and rain Fresh deluge of wet weather comes after Storm Austen brought strong winds to many regions on Friday Pol Allingham and Helen William, Press Association Sat 24 Oct 2026 18.40 EDT Last modified on Sat 24 Oct 2026 19.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Amber weather warnings have come into force as the worst of Storm Boelo could be set to hit parts of the UK. Storm Boelo’s winds will peak from Saturday evening, leaving areas in the warning zone, including Scotland, parts of Northern Ireland and the far north of England, braced for gusts of 60-70mph and even 80mph in exposed coastal spots, the Met Office said. The forecaster’s amber warnings came into force on Saturday at 9pm. Maximum gust speeds of 75mph have already hit South Uist Range, Western Isles, Highland and Eilean Siar, Scotland on Saturday, according to the Met Office, which has also issued several yellow warnings for rain. Storm Boelo follows Storm Austen , the first named storm of the season, which brought strong winds to parts of the UK on Friday. Gusts of 76mph were recorded at St Mary’s airport in the Isles of Scilly, with 74mph at Aberporth in south-west Wales and 71mph at Culdrose in Cornwall. Heavy downpours since 8am on Saturday have already seen rainfall totals of 72mm in White Barrow, Wiltshire, along with 43mm in both Cwm Dyli, just south of the Snowdon range in North Wales, and Inveruglas on the west shore of Loch Lomond, Scotland. View image in fullscreen Waves crash over the lighthouse at Newhaven Harbour in East Sussex during Storm Austen on Friday. Photograph: Toby Melville/Reuters Hundreds of homes were still without power in south-west England after Storm Austen hit the region on Friday where the National Grid said power had been restored to 131,225 properties by Saturday at 7pm. An amber wind warning, the Met Office’s second most severe, is active across Scotland, the north of England down to Carlisle from 9pm on Saturday to the same time on Sunday. A further amber warning runs from 9pm on Saturday to 10am on Sunday in the north-east of Northern Ireland. Storm Boelo, the second named storm of the season, will bring a danger to life from flying debris and crashing waves and people should stay indoors as much as possible, the forecaster said. The amber warning sits within wider yellow wind warnings which extend south into parts of England and North Wales and cover the whole of Northern Ireland. The Environment Agency had issued 58 alerts for spots across England where flooding is possible by 8pm on Saturday, as well as 12 warnings stating that flooding is expected. Met Office chief forecaster Jason Kelly said: “Storm Boelo will be felt across the UK this weekend, with the strongest winds and greatest potential for disruption in the north. “Amber warnings are in place across mainland Scotland, parts of Northern Ireland and the far north of England, where gusts of 60-70mph are expected widely, with the potential for 80mph in exposed coastal locations. “Strong winds will also affect other parts of the UK, with gusts of 50-60mph possible in places. Heavy rain will provide an additional hazard, particularly in the north, bringing the potential for further impacts. “People should prepare for the potential for disruption, particularly to travel and power supplies.” People should secure loose items outside, plan ahead if they are travelling and keep an eye on the latest forecast and warnings, he advised. View image in fullscreen The wet weather did not deter shoppers in Oxford Street, central London, on Saturday. Photograph: Maja Smiejkowska/PA Storm Boelo has already caused widespread disruption. Boelo’s strong winds disrupted flights at Dublin airport, where as of 4pm on Saturday, nine outbound and 10 inbound flights had been cancelled by airlines because of weather issues. It also reported that six inbound flights performed go-arounds – five of which landed on the second attempt, with the other diverting to another airport before returning a short time later. Network Rail shared images of a trampoline beneath a train and a shed by the tracks, in a call for those living near rail lines to secure their garden furniture firmly. Visit Liverpool announced that the region’s River of Light event, featuring illuminated artwork, had been cancelled “in the interests of safety”. London’s annual Diwali on the Square celebrations this Sunday were also cancelled on independent health and safety experts’ recommendations in light of the storm. Other attractions closed on Sunday include Edinburgh Castle and the Fountains Abbey estate in North Yorkshire, which was due to host its Fountains by Floodlight event. https://www.theguardian.com/world/ng-int.text: Brazil Brazil election 2026: Full second round results as Lula wins comeback against Flávio Bolsonaro After a shock defeat in the first round, the incumbent Brazilian president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, has turned the election around to win the runoff. Live blog: latest analysis and reaction Seán Clarke and Tom Phillips Sun 25 Oct 2026 20.15 EDT First published on Sun 25 Oct 2026 15.37 EDT Share Live second round results Last updated at 21:00:41 BRT With 88.7% of districts counted Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva 51.52% Workers' party (PT) | 56,506,197 votes Flávio Bolsonaro 48.48% Liberal party (PL) | 53,164,037 votes Guardian graphic. Source: TSE Results by state How the election works Brazil’s president is elected purely by the popular vote. A winning candidate needs one more vote than 50% of votes cast; there is no role for the parliament and no electoral college. Because no candidate achieved 50% in the first round on 4 October, the two leading candidates go into a runoff. One of them is Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva , the incumbent leftwing president, commonly known as Lula. The other, and the leading candidate in the first round, is Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of the far-right former president Jair Bolsonaro. Bolsonaro senior is serving a 27-year prison sentence for plotting a failed coup attempt after he lost to Lula in the 2022 election, but has endorsed his son and hopes to be released if he wins. Bolsonaro junior is a lawyer and former senator from Rio. In 2022, Lula beat Jair Bolsonaro in the second round, with an electoral base concentrated in the north-east of the country, while Bolsonaro led in the south. But on that occasion Lula entered the second round as the leading candidate from the first round, and won the bellwether state of Minas Gerais, north of Rio de Janeiro. In the first round of the 2026 election, Bolsonaro beat Lula in Minas Gerais by 48.43% to 43.33%. Never, since the return of democracy to Brazil in 1985, has the first round runner-up managed to turn the game around and win the second vote. But Lula’s campaign has been buoyed by massive, student-led anti-Bolsonaro protests after the first round and hopes to stage a historic fightback on Sunday. Lula is already the longest-serving president in Brazil’s modern history, serving two terms from 2003 to 2010, before returning to office in 2023. He will turn 81 on Tuesday. Bolsonaro is 45.
